@AndersBroman many thanks for the explanation. Could you please show me an example?

I am a newbie Wireshark contributor, and I am kind of new to this. 

I have read through the hf_ structure_

```
struct _header_field_info {
    /* ---------- set by dissector --------- */
    const char        *name;              /**< [FIELDNAME] full name of this field */
    const char        *abbrev;            /**< [FIELDFILTERNAME] filter name of this field */
    enum ftenum        type;              /**< [FIELDTYPE] field type, one of FT_ (from ftypes.h) */
    int                display;           /**< [FIELDDISPLAY] one of BASE_, or field bit-width if FT_BOOLEAN and non-zero bitmask */
    const void        *strings;           /**< [FIELDCONVERT] value_string, val64_string, range_string or true_false_string,
                                               typically converted by VALS(), RVALS() or TFS().
                                               If this is an FT_PROTOCOL or BASE_PROTOCOL_INFO then it points to the
                                               associated protocol_t structure */
    uint64_t           bitmask;           /**< [BITMASK] bitmask of interesting bits */
    const char        *blurb;             /**< [FIELDDESCR] Brief description of field */
```
but I have not seen the formatter option.

> As for the 1/4 values are they guaranteed to always be in steps of 4?

The standard says 1/4 sec and day per bit:
https://www.isobus.net/isobus/pGNAndSPN/16061?type=PGN

For `snprintf`, the second parameter is the size of the buffer (including the null terminator). It will write no more than `bufsz - 1` characters, not including the null terminator. Even though the minute offset is supposed to be in the range -59 to 59, when retrieving a value from packet data it is possible to have a larger result with a three digit decimal number, in which case the "n" of "min" will not be written.

It would be fine to have "9" instead of "8" for bufsiz here, since your buffer is 9 bytes long, but this is also simply a good reason to avoid `snprintf`, as it demonstrates that people have a really hard time remembering how it works.
